source.title: Rank-1 LoRAs Encode Interpretable Reasoning Signals
source.authors: Jake Ward; P. Riechers; Adam Shai

record.tranche_reason: The study uses automated interpretation and classification to measure monosemanticity in Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct adapter activations and base-model MLP neurons, a different method and model from the claim's audit.
record.gate_note: The study reports monosemanticity-classification shares for LoRA activations and sampled MLP neurons in Figure 1. Benchmark performance and ablation results do not measure the claim versions about neuron interpretability and are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: As a baseline, the study classifies about 3,840 MLP neurons of Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct (the first 60 per layer) as monosemantic, fuzzy or polysemantic. It uses gpt-5-mini autointerpretation of the top 64 activating contexts. This gives a per-neuron share in a different model from the original audit, by a different method, so it bears on V2. The LoRA-direction and SAE results concern adapter directions, not neurons.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly correct. The authors conclude that rank-1 LoRA directions are roughly as often monosemantic as MLP neurons, which they call a positive result. They also conclude that an SAE over the LoRA state yields more monosemantic features (62%), and they caution that LLM autointerpretation may miss features' true roles. They draw no conclusion about neuron interpretability as such; the MLP neurons serve only as a baseline.
record.recipe_differences: Uses LLM-generated interpretations from top-activating contexts and LLM classification of those interpretations; does not report held-out activation prediction. It compares LoRA directions with sampled MLP neurons rather than auditing neuron poles as in the claim.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper notes that SAE feature categorization is subjective and sensitive to prompt wording.

fits_no_version.finding: Rank-1 LoRA adapter directions classify as 22.4% monosemantic, 49.1% fuzzy and 28.5% polysemantic, similar to the MLP neurons.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Directions in a fine-tuning adapter are about as interpretable as base-model neurons.

fits_no_version.finding: Of about 2000 cross-layer SAE features over the LoRA activation state, 62% are classified 'cleanly monosemantic' and 22% 'broad but consistent'. This is text only, with no row.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE features over adapter activations are more often monosemantic than individual neurons or adapter directions.

record.problems: The monosemanticity judgments rely on LLM autointerpretation and autocategorization, which the authors describe as subjective and potentially inaccurate. The comparison uses only one model and the first 60 neurons of each MLP; the paper gives no uncertainty estimates for the plotted percentages.
record.rows_left_out: No additional results relevant to the tested claim version were omitted.

untested.parts: Only one dense model (Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct) and only the first 60 neurons per layer are examined. No mixture-of-experts models, no scale range, no trillion-parameter models. Only top activations are examined, not both poles. There is no separate 'two related jobs' category and no layer breakdown.
Explanations are judged only on the activating examples. There is no test of prediction on held-out text.

record.verdict_notes: The record's reading of r4 as 'absent' (20.2% vs 90%) compares the strict category 0 alone with the claim. This overstates the contrast, because category 1 still requires every example to fit one explanation. Neuron sampling is the first 60 indices per layer, not random. No uncertainty is reported.

versions.untested_parts: The Qwen3-32B audit and its stated shares of neuron poles are not examined.

Only Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct is examined; the study does not test other model sizes, mixture-of-experts models, or models up to trillions of parameters. It reports monosemanticity classifications, not the claimed one-job/two-related-jobs/ununderstood breakdown.
InceptionV1's cat-and-car example and recursive generalization are not examined.
The stated architecture, regularization, and tool explanations and the estimates for InceptionV1-sized vision models are not tested.
Attribution graphs and reconstruction using a model's own neurons are not tested.
The study interprets max-activating examples but does not test explanations on separate activations to assess predictive failures.
The study does not score explanations by simulating activations on new text.

relation.reason: The MLP-neuron baseline gives a share of neurons with a consistent explanation, which bears on V2. The paper's main aim is LoRA interpretation.

tranche.reason: It uses a different method (LLM autointerpretation of top-64 contexts, 3-way monosemanticity class) to measure the share of interpretable MLP neurons in another model, as a baseline for LoRA directions.

source_check.notes: Figure 1 values are bar labels in the figure text. The pairing is fixed because each series sums to 100% (LoRA 22.4/49.1/28.5; MLP 20.2/46.9/32.9). 'First 60 neurons of each MLP' is stated; the total (~3,840) is not. The caption calls the sample 'arbitrarily sampled', and there is no uncertainty or count per class. The 'subjective and prompt-sensitive' caveat concerns the Fig. 2 functional categories, not the 0/1/2 classification. The Appendix B prompts are the method's own prompts, not instructions to a reader.

statements.correction: Sec. 3.1: 'this categorization methodology is subjective and sensitive to prompt verbiage' refers to the LLM-generated functional categories plotted in Fig. 2 (category-wise activation densities). For the 3-way classification, the only caveat is in Limitations: LLM autointerpretation and autocategorization may often fail to uncover features' 'true' role. 20.2% / 46.9% / 32.9% (MLP neurons, Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct) are correct.
statements.problem: Misattributed caveat: the authors call the functional-category scheme (Fig. 2) subjective and prompt-sensitive. They do not say this of the gpt-5-mini 0/1/2 monosemanticity classification.

statements.correction: Of the sampled MLP neurons of Qwen-2.5-32B-Instruct, 20.2% are class 0 (specific) and 46.9% class 1 (broad but all examples fit), together 67.1%. 32.9% are class 2 (polysemantic). All three are shares of all sampled neurons (Fig. 1).
statements.problem: '67.1% ..., of which 20.2% are strictly specific' gives the wrong base. 20.2% is a share of all sampled neurons, not of the 67.1%.

statements.correction: 20.2% (class 0) and 67.1% (class 0 + class 1, 46.9%) are right. The authors call the functional categorization of features (Fig. 2) subjective and prompt-sensitive. In Limitations they say autointerpretation/autocategorization may miss features' 'true' role. They report no test of how sensitive the 0/1/2 classification is to the prompt.
statements.problem: The numbers are right, but the authors' 'subjective and sensitive to prompt verbiage' remark is about the Fig. 2 functional categorization. It is not about the strict-vs-fuzzy class boundary or the monosemanticity judge prompt, so it does not support this factor as written.

statements.correction: The 'subjective and sensitive to prompt verbiage' caveat applies to the LLM-generated functional categories (Fig. 2). Limitations add that autointerpretation may miss features' 'true' role. The SAE (batch-top-k, k=16, expansion 8) is trained on the 448-dim LoRA activation state. It has roughly 2000 features: 62% 'cleanly monosemantic' (vs 22% of LoRA directions) and 22% 'broad but consistent'. All other numbers (20.2/46.9/32.9; 22.4/49.1/28.5) are correct.
statements.problem: Right after the 3-way split, it says the authors call 'their categorisation' subjective and prompt-sensitive. That remark is about the Fig. 2 functional categories, not the monosemanticity classes. f1 also omits that the SAE is trained on the 448-dim LoRA activation state, not on model neurons.
